question: Published evidence for a UEFA forecaster prior: carry-over weight, early-season blending, UEFA-specific results
note: Researcher output plus one skeptic per topic. Every claim carries a verbatim quote, URL and read date; a claim whose skeptic verdict is not confirmed carries that verdict and note and must be read with it. External evidence only: none of it is FIELD data, and none of these sources was used for data.

claims.quantity: Out-of-sample RPS x100 = 19.729 for a static pre-season Elo (ClubElo, read on 1 September, never updated in-season) versus 23.068 for an expanding-window outcome-frequency benchmark; 600 evaluation matches (2023/24 and 2024/25), of which 272 are 2024/25 league-phase matches. Elo alone explains R2 = 0.237 of goal difference. An equal-weight pool of Elo and prior-season Transfermarkt squad value scores 19.431; versus Elo alone the difference is -0.297 x100 RPS (SE 0.148, p = 0.045).
claims.context: UEFA Champions League and Europa League only (no Conference League), 1,503 matches 2020/21-2024/25, evaluation on the last two seasons. The paper states no within-season information from the forecast season is used to update the models, so this measures how good a purely carried-over prior is on UEFA matches. It does not say how a prior should be weighted against n current-season matches. Authors per the arXiv abstract page: Gergely Csurilla and Laszlo Csato. Preprint, v1 2026-09-18; I do not know its peer-review status. No evident commercial interest. Quote is two table rows (ordered-probit table) joined by a space.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Numbers and quote reproduce exactly. Table 5c (ordered probit) has Historical 23.068 and Elo 19.729. Table 6 has Equal-weight vs Elo -0.297, SE 0.148, p 0.045. The evaluation is 238 + 362 = 600 matches. The Table 3 league-phase count is 272. The Table 5a R2 is 0.237. Authors and the 2026-09-18 date match. The framing overreaches in four ways. (1) 'Purely carried-over prior' is wrong. The paper uses ClubElo 'observed on 1 September'. Csato's 2023 paper says ClubElo is 'continuously updated once a match is played', so a 1 Sept rating already contains qualifiers and early league matches. Only 'not updated within the forecast season' holds. (2) 'Elo alone explains R2 = 0.237' is out-of-sample R2 of an Elo-plus-match-context-controls model against an expanding-window mean. The paper says the Historical benchmark has no controls and calls the Elo/TM/pool comparison the substantive one. I could not size the effect. It is probably small, since outcome frequencies already carry average home advantage, but that is my inference. (3) The quoted sample is the common Elo-TM sample of 1,394 matches, not 1,503. (4) p = 0.045 is one of several uncorrected pairwise tests. The paper says pooling is best overall but 'not in either season separately', that the ranking changes across seasons, and that pooling versus Transfermarkt alone is uncertain (p = 0.499). Usable as numbers; do not call it a pure carry-over test.

claims.quantity: Season-to-season correlation of points per game r = 0.70 (95% interval 0.67 to 0.72) across 1,997 same-league club pairs; goal difference r = 0.74. By league (season-to-season correlation of points per game): Premier League 0.74, La Liga 0.80, Serie A 0.77, Bundesliga 0.63, Ligue 1 0.64, Championship 0.33. Luck share of the spread in points per game: 26% at 38 games, 72% at 5, 56% at 10, 41% at 19, 15% at 76.
claims.context: Six domestic leagues (five top flights plus the English Championship), 49,615 league matches, 2005-06 to 2025-26, from football-data.co.uk. Domestic leagues, not UEFA competitions. Persistence uses only clubs that stayed in the same division (relegated and promoted clubs excluded), which likely overstates persistence for the whole population; the page says so. These are observed-points correlations, so they are diluted by match luck. Site author Cheng Xu, a practitioner (research page, published 2026-10-23); I did not determine whether the site has a commercial interest. The by-league figures are in the page's table, not in the quoted sentences.
claims.quote: Across 1,997 clubs that stayed in the same league, points per game correlated 0.70 from one season to the next (95% interval 0.67 to 0.72). Goal difference, the underlying measure, persisted slightly more (0.74).
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Quote is verbatim on the page. The 0.70 (0.67 to 0.72) and 0.74 figures, the five-row luck-share table (72/56/41/26/15) and the six-league table (22/24/22/28/29/36 percent luck; 0.74/0.80/0.77/0.63/0.64/0.33) all match. Author Cheng Xu and the 2026-10-23 date are correct. Minor points: the page lists the same-division restriction as a limitation but does not say it 'overstates' persistence; that inference is the researcher's. '1,997 clubs' is the page's wording; 'club pairs' is the researcher's gloss. The Method line says by-games luck shares come from rescaling the luck variance by number of matches (see missedEvidence on the circular check).

claims.quantity: Between-season forgetting factor for surviving teams omega_b = 0.770, 0.795 and 0.737 in the three fitted Bayesian state-space variants, against a within-season (per round) forgetting factor omega = 0.988, 0.985 and 0.987. Third numeric column in the quoted rows is omega_b; the second is omega.
claims.context: English Premier League only. Maximum-likelihood estimates fitted on the first 18 EPL seasons (1992/93-2009/10) and tested on 2010/11-2023/24. Per the paper, omega multiplies the Gamma hyper-parameters, 'conserving its mean ... but increasing its variance', so omega_b discounts the weight (information content) of last season's state at the summer break by about 20-26%; it is not a regression of the mean toward the league average. It is not directly comparable with an Elo carry-over coefficient. The paper also states that a newly promoted side's performance 'does not have a strong dependence' on its lower-league history. Peer-reviewed (JRSS Series C, 2025). No evident commercial interest.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: The OUP full text has the table with header omega_h, omega, omega_b, omega_hb. Rows are 0.999/0.988/0.770, 0.999/0.985/0.795 and 0.999/0.987/0.737. Training is seasons 1992/93-2009/10 and test is 2010/11-2023/24. The Gamma extend step multiplies p and q by omega, 'conserving its mean ... but increasing its variance'. The promoted-side sentence is verbatim ('does not have a strong dependence on the promoted side's history'). Peer-review status is correct (JRSS C 74(3), published online 2024-12-21, 'Conflicts of interest: None declared'). Caveats: the quoted two rows do not contain 0.737/0.987, which sit in the third row of the same table. 'Per round' is not the page's wording. By my arithmetic the variance multiplier 1/omega_b is 1.26 to 1.36, about 19 to 25 rounds of within-season forgetting at omega 0.988. It is not a regression of the mean, as the researcher says.

claims.quantity: Exponential time-decay constant k = 0.001824 per day for down-weighting past matches in a weighted-likelihood EPL model, half-life 380 days. By my arithmetic (not in the paper) a match one year old keeps about 0.51 of the weight of a match played today.
claims.context: English Premier League, univariate Poisson model, k chosen to minimise out-of-sample RPS over seasons 1996/97-2009/10. This is the weight of old data in a model that also uses current-season data, so it is the closest published analogue to a prior-versus-current blend, but it is a time decay and not a season-boundary regression factor. Domestic league, not UEFA competitions. Peer-reviewed (JRSS Series C, 2025).
claims.quote: This resulted in a decay constant of $k=0.001824$ corresponding to a half-life of 380 days.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Quote is verbatim: 'This resulted in a decay constant of k=0.001824 corresponding to a half-life of 380 days.' It was fitted by minimising RPS of the univariate Poisson over 1996/97-2009/10, as stated. ln2/0.001824 = 380.0 days and exp(-0.001824 x 365) = 0.514, so 'about 0.51' holds. The researcher correctly flags that this is a time decay, not a season-boundary regression.

claims.quantity: Elo season-boundary carry-over = 0.90 of the distance from 1500 retained (10% regression per summer) was the best of 720 tuned settings (K 20, home advantage 40, promoted sides start at 1550, margin counted); tuned Elo test log loss 0.945, equal to Dixon-Coles 0.945, bookmaker 0.932.
claims.context: The page says 'Premiership' and tells readers to download the 'Premiership file (SC0)' for 2000/01-2025/26. I infer SC0 is football-data.co.uk's code for the Scottish top flight; the page does not say 'Scottish' in the text I read. Tuned on held-back seasons 2016/17-2020/21, tested on 2021/22-2025/26. Carry-over regresses toward a fixed 1500, not toward the league mean, and interacts with K = 20. Domestic league, not UEFA. Educational site (author Bryan McGuire, 'Machine Learning Through Football', Part 13, published 2026-09-30); I did not determine whether it has a commercial interest.
claims.quote: The winner: K 20, home advantage 40, 90% carry-over, promoted sides start at 1550, margin counted.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Quote is verbatim. The test table (Elo 0.945, Dixon-Coles 0.945, bookmaker 0.932; held-back 2016/17-2020/21, test 2021/22-2025/26) matches. The 720 grid is 4 x 6 x 5 x 3 x 2. The code regresses toward a fixed 1500. The page says 'Premiership' and 'SC0' and never says Scottish, so the researcher's inference stands. I could not independently fetch the football-data.co.uk code list (blocked). SC0 as the Scottish top flight is my domain knowledge, so it is unverified in this read. Caveat the researcher under-weights: the page says 'Only two dials are pinned down: K ... and home advantage'. Carry-over is not identified, so 0.9 is a flat-valley winner and a weak design anchor. The page also notes the best settings shift between eras.

claims.quantity: 63 of 720 settings scored within 0.001 log loss of the best on the held-back seasons, and those 63 span carry-over values from 0.8 to 0.95.
claims.context: The grid only tried carry-over values 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95 and 1.0 (dials table: 'Carry-over 0.8 to 1'), so the 0.8 lower end is the grid floor and values below 0.8 were not tested; the data do not show whether 0.7 or 0.5 would also be in the flat region. Same scope and caveats as C5 (Scottish top flight inferred from the SC0 file code; domestic; K = 20).
claims.quote: 63 of the 720 score within 0.001 of the best, and between them they include every promoted start tried, margin counted and not counted, and carry-over from 0.8 to 0.95.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Quote is verbatim. The code grid is (0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95, 1.0), so 0.8 is the floor and nothing below it was tried. The stated range of the 63 near-best settings is 0.8 to 0.95, so full carry-over (1.0) is outside the flat valley by the page's own wording. The researcher did not use this point. Same Scottish-top-flight, domestic and K = 20 caveats as C5.

claims.quantity: Coefficient on last season's Elo (ELO last season) = 0.701 (SE 0.07, Arellano-Bond difference GMM) and 0.697 (SE 0.05, Blundell-Bond system GMM) in the baseline specifications (1) and (2); 1.134 and 0.979 in the specifications with interaction terms (3) and (4).
claims.context: Dynamic panel on ClubElo ratings taken on the last day of July, 2001-2025; 140 clubs in 26 countries that appear across the whole period (clubs 'consistently top'), so survivorship likely raises persistence. Dependent variable is the Elo level with other covariates (league dispersion, finishing-position dummies, GDP), so this is an autoregressive coefficient of a full year of Elo, which already includes a season of in-season updating; it is not the same quantity as a carry-over factor applied at the season boundary. Includes UEFA-competition results through ClubElo but is not specific to them. I saw the table through the search extract of the paper's PDF; the column text is garbled and the specification labels (1)-(4) come from the paper's own description. Journal paper (Warsaw Forum of Economic Sociology, 2025).
claims.quote: Table 3. Estimation results for a full samplE (2000/2001-2024/2025) (1) (2) (3) (4) ELO (last season) 0.701 *** 0.697 *** 1.134 *** 0.979 ***
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Table 3 row reads 'ELO (last season) 0.701 *** 0.697 *** 1.134 *** 0.979 ***' with SE row (0.07) (0.05) (0.24) (0.14). Specs (1) and (3) are Arellano-Bond and (2) and (4) Blundell-Bond. Elo is taken on the last day of July for 2001-2025. There are 140 clubs in 26 countries, included only if present across the whole period. The source is ClubElo (Schiefler 2025). The journal is Warsaw Forum of Economic Sociology 16(32), Autumn 2025. Missing caveats: the GMM specs use club fixed effects and year effects ('twoway'), so 0.70 is persistence of within-club deviations, not regression toward a league mean. In specs (3) and (4) the 1.134 and 0.979 belong to the benchmark rank-9-to-12 group. The Top4 x ELO interactions (-0.444, -0.279) put the effective Top4 slope near 0.69 and 0.70, consistent with the baseline. Conclusion text says 'success has bred success'.

claims.quantity: FiveThirtyEight/ESPN SPI preseason rating = 2/3 end-of-season SPI + 1/3 SPI implied by Transfermarkt market value (a 67% / 33% split, as reported by the summary). Same deck reports a ranked probability score improvement of 0.0011 from adding market value to the preseason rating (versus 0.0018 for expected-goals metrics and 0.0006 for match importance).
claims.context: Third-party summary (a university reading-group slide deck, 2023-04-28) of the model owner's methodology; I could NOT read FiveThirtyEight's own methodology page (the URL now redirects to an ABC News politics page). A forum copy of the 538 article text that I did read gives the sentence 'ratings at the end of the previous season, and its market value as calculated by Transfermarkt' but contains no 67/33 numbers, so the weights are third-party-reported only (blog and thesis snippets repeat them; I did not read those pages). Domestic leagues plus 538's league-strength adjustment for inter-league matches. The model owner is a media organisation (ESPN/ABC) with no evident commercial stake in this design question. The 2/3 blends two inputs; it is not a pure carry-over coefficient.
claims.quote: 2/3 × end-of-season’s SPI + 1/3 × SPI implied by market value
claims.label: third-party-report
claims.skepticNote: The 'third-party-report' label is correct. The deck text is verbatim: '2/3 x end-of-season's SPI + 1/3 x SPI implied by market value'. It also gives 'Current RPS = 0.1957 after reductions' of 0.0018 (expected goals), 0.0011 (market values) and 0.0006 (match importance). I reproduced the block on 538's own page: fivethirtyeight.com redirects to an ABC News politics page and the Wayback copy is 'CONTENT_NOT_CACHED'. The same 67/33 split appears in search snippets of an Erasmus MSc thesis (thesis.eur.nl/pub/62828, '67% influence ... 33% influence'), the dadmetrics blog (2019) and a Goalside post (2023). All are secondary and may share one upstream. The 2/3 is a blend weight, not a carry-over coefficient, as the researcher says.

claims.quantity: In EPL team-seasons, a squad-stability index (share of the squad also at the club a year earlier; mean 62.6%, SD 12.8, range 30.3-92.0%) adds a standardised coefficient beta = 0.14 (p = .015) for league points on top of past performance, whose coefficient magnitude is 0.63 (R2 = .47; df 177). Raw correlation of league rank between consecutive seasons r = .71 (n = 180).
claims.context: English Premier League 1998/99-2006/07 (9 seasons x 20 clubs = 180 team-seasons); also covers Italian Serie A. The stability effect is an additive term; the extract shows no test of whether turnover changes the prior-performance coefficient (no interaction), so this is only indirect evidence that carry-over is weaker after heavy squad change. The extract prints a negative beta for past performance on points, and the variable coding is not visible in the extract. Whether the manuscript was peer-reviewed is not shown. Manager stability is reported as an independent but weaker effect (page text, no figure quoted here).
claims.quote: number of points (R2 = .47, team stability: β = 0.14, t(177) = 2.45, p = .015; past performance: β = -0.63, t(177) = -10.89, p = 1.0E-99)
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Verbatim string (R2 = .47; team stability beta = 0.14, t(177) = 2.45, p = .015; past performance beta = -0.63, t(177) = -10.89). Superscript spacing differs in the extract only. Stability index is mean 62.6, SD 12.8, range 30.3-92.0, defined as the share of the squad also at the club at the start of the previous season. Data are EPL 1998/9-2006/7, nine seasons of 20 teams. Serie A and the English Second Division are secondary. Corrections: the paper defines past performance as 'ranking in previous season', so the negative beta on points is expected from the coding. The researcher said the coding was not visible. The r = .71 sentence is worded as league ranks 'in 2001/2 and 2002/3: r(178) = .71'. df 178 implies a pooled n = 180, so the researcher's 'n = 180' is an inference from df. This is an unpublished manuscript ('Running Head' format); peer-review status is not shown.

claims.quantity: Model-output scenario values for a new manager in the EPL: season performance falls by 1.05 league points when the departing manager's tenure was short (at most two seasons) and by 4.64 points when it was long (five seasons or more). The same page gives -3.73 points for 'instability in terms of changes in players' (high net transfer spending with reduced wages, or vice versa); that sentence is on the page but not in the quote.
claims.context: Bayesian network for pre-season prediction of EPL league points. The page itself calls squad instability and managerial ability 'expert variables', so these figures are outputs of a model whose structure and parts of whose parameters are expert-specified; they are NOT independent empirical estimates of how carry-over weakens, and I did not see the sample size in the extract. Domestic league only. Peer-reviewed (Knowledge-Based Systems, 2017). The authors also state that managerial change 'does not appear to have as much of an impact' as other factors.
claims.quote: Specifically, when a new manager joins a club, in conjunction with the departing manager's longevity with the club being Low (i.e. maximum of two season), a team's performance declines by 1.05 points. Interestingly, when the longevity of the departing manager is High (i.e. five seasons or more) the loss in performance is 4.64 points.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Quote and numbers are verbatim (1.05, 4.64, 3.73 and the 'does not appear to have as much of an impact' sentence). The context claim is not supported: 'NOT independent empirical estimates ... expert-parameterised'. The paper says CPTs of the data variables 'are directly learned from data', and the expert nodes (Squad instability, Managerial ability) 'do not influence the data-driven expectations, as long as they remain unobserved'. The New Manager and Longevity scenarios are data variables, with manager data recorded from MyFootballFacts for EPL seasons around 2000/01-2014/15. So the -1.05 and -4.64 are probably data-learned outputs of an expert-structured Bayesian network, not expert-set parameters. I did not find a stated sample size or confirm that the expert nodes were unobserved for those scenarios. They are still scenario effects on expected season points, not a carry-over coefficient. Designs that call them 'expert-parameterised' (designImplication item 6) should say 'BN-conditional EPL scenario outputs'.

topics.designImplication: Evidence-supported range (all domestic-league evidence except C1; none of it is FIELD data). 1) Boundary carry-over on last season's rating deviation: the published figures span about 0.7 to 0.9, meaning 10-30% regression toward the mean. Anchors: tuned Elo carry-over 0.9 with a flat region 0.8-0.95 (C5, C6; grid floor 0.8, so lower values untested), the EPL state-space model's summer information discount of 0.74-0.80 (C3), and an Elo autoregressive coefficient of 0.70 (C7). 0.80 is the only value that touches all three ranges, but they measure different things (an Elo carry factor, an information discount, a full-year Elo AR coefficient), so I would not treat that as convergence. I found nothing published that supports a value below 0.7. 2) Persistence of observed points per game is r = 0.70 (0.63-0.80 by top league; 0.33 in the Championship), goal difference 0.74 (C2). 3) A pure carried-over prior is valuable on UEFA matches: static 1-September Elo gets RPS 0.197 against 0.231 for outcome frequencies on 600 UEFA matches, and pooling it equally with prior-season squad value gains a further 0.003 RPS versus Elo alone (p = 0.045) (C1). That supports a second prior input, but C1 never updates within a season, so it says nothing about how fast n current matches should take over. 4) DERIVED BY ME, NOT PUBLISHED, UNTESTED ON UEFA: from the C2 page's luck shares (26% at 38 games, scaled by 1/n) and the 0.70 correlation, a normal-normal model gives per-match noise = 0.26 x 38 = 9.88 (in units of total points-per-game variance) and a prior-residual variance of (1 - 0.26) - 0.70^2 = 0.25, so the prior is worth about 9.88 / 0.25 = 40 matches. Check: that noise term reproduces the page's published luck shares at 5, 10, 19 and 76 games (72.7, 57.2, 41.3, 14.9% against 72, 56, 41, 15%), within about 1.2 points. With n current matches the current-season weight is n / (n + 40): about 7% at n = 3, 11% at 5, 15% at 7, 17% at 8. Using each league's own luck share and correlation gives a prior worth about 33 to 76 matches in the top five leagues (Bundesliga 33, Premier League 36, Ligue 1 37, Serie A 45, La Liga 76) and about 26 in the Championship, so that figure is sensitive to rounding in the inputs. 5) Caveats on transfer to FIELD: the matches are cross-league, so rating spread is wider than inside one league and the current-season signal is stronger than this derivation assumes; last season's domestic rating then needs a league-strength bridge that this evidence does not quantify; and 3-7 matches against varying opponents are noisier than the league-season averages used here. 6) Manager and squad change: the evidence is thin and indirect (an additive squad-stability effect of beta 0.14 against 0.63 for past performance in 180 EPL team-seasons, C9; expert-parameterised model outputs of -1.05 to -4.64 points, C10). There is no published, verified turnover-conditional carry-over weight, so I would not build one. 7) Because the weight must come from external evidence, the defensible pre-registered options are a carry factor in 0.7-0.9 and a prior worth roughly 30-80 current-season-equivalent matches (derived, point value about 40), with FIELD's own data used only to test the choice.

missedEvidence: UEFA-specific evidence the researcher said did not exist: Csato, 'Club coefficients in the UEFA Champions League: Time for shift to an Elo-based formula' (arXiv 2304.09078v6; Taylor & Francis 10.1080/24748668.2023.2274221). ClubElo is fixed at 30 June each year (a cleaner pure carried-over prior than C1's 1 September rating) over 19 Champions League seasons 2003/04-2021/22 and 1,824 group matches. Elo gives 73.32% accuracy for decisive group matches, McFadden R2 0.121 in the multinomial with draws, and AUC 0.814. Elo beats the five-season UEFA coefficient, which adds nothing once Elo is included for group matches and knockout ties (it adds a little for group ranking). The paper also states ClubElo is 'continuously updated once a match is played', which supports the point that a 1 September rating is not purely carried over. It gives no carry-over coefficient or prior-versus-n weighting.

C1's own table contradicts a 'second prior input' reading of Elo alone: Transfermarkt alone scores RPS 19.533 against Elo 19.729 (Success 0.577 vs 0.558). Equal-weight versus Transfermarkt alone is -0.102, p = 0.499. The ranking changes by season (Transfermarkt best in 2024/25; the joint model best in 2023/24). The Elo versus log-Transfermarkt correlation is 0.877. The researcher quoted only the one p = 0.045 contrast.

The luck-vs-skill page has directly measured early-form figures the researcher did not use: points per game after 5 games explains 25% of remaining-matches variation, and 39% after 19 games. The researcher's own noise/skill split (9.88 and 0.74, from the same page) predicts only 19.4% (5 v 33 games) and 34.5% (19 v 19). Fitting the page's 25% and 39% implies per-match noise of about 6.8 to 8.5 rather than 9.88, which gives a prior worth roughly 27 to 34 matches rather than 40. This is my arithmetic, not a published result. The researcher's 'check' that the noise term reproduces the published luck shares (72/56/41/15%) is circular, because the page produces those shares by rescaling the same luck variance by 1/n (Method section).

The researcher's other derived arithmetic does reproduce: n0 = 39.5; weights 7.1%, 11.2%, 15.0% and 16.8% at n = 3, 5, 7 and 8; league-level figures 36, 76, 45, 33, 37 and 26. The 1/n luck shares recompute to 72.8, 57.2, 41.3 and 14.9% (the researcher wrote 72.7 for the first). But C2 also implies true-talent season-to-season persistence of about 0.70 / 0.74 = 0.946 (observed r divided by skill share, my arithmetic, ignoring the promoted/relegated exclusion). That is above the researcher's 'evidence-supported' 0.7 to 0.9 carry-factor range, and the 0.70 is luck-diluted, so it is not a carry factor.

A second, assumption-laden route to a prior of roughly the same size, which I computed and which is not published: Ridall et al.'s k = 0.001824 per day applied to 38 matches per season spread over about 275 days gives an effective past-data mass of about 52 match-equivalents at season start (about 47 after 8 current matches). It is weights in a likelihood, not a normal-normal prior, so treat it as a plausibility cross-check only.

My inference: a UEFA league phase has 8 (or 6) matches per club, fewer than the roughly 10 match days at which convergence starts, so a current-season-only rating would not be expected to match a prior-using rating anywhere inside a league phase.

topics.designImplication: Inference from the evidence above, not a finding. (1) A prior is not optional for an 8-match phase: a current-season-only model needed about 10 match days (of 34-38) to approach prior-using models (T2-01), and in the Bundesliga previous-season information still improved the estimate after 17 matches (T2-02). (2) The published, quotable form of the blend is shrinkage: estimate = (n*observed + m*prior)/(n+m). The only quantified m values are descriptive and domestic: about 11 matches (Scottish points per game, T2-07), about 14 (Bundesliga goal difference per match, T2-03) and about 21 (Bundesliga points, T2-03). All three are for a league-mean prior; an informative carried-over prior has smaller residual variance, so by the same algebra its m is larger than these. They bound m rather than fix it, depend on how widely true quality is spread in the league, and none was validated on forecast loss or on UEFA competitions, so the UEFA value must still be argued from external spread-of-quality evidence (none found) and tested on FIELD's reserved data. (3) Time decay is a separate dial: Dixon-Coles (about 373-day half-life, T2-06) and Ley et al. (390 days, T2-05) agree for league clubs, and sparse-match settings preferred much longer half-lives (3 years for national teams), which suggests a decay half-life of at least about a year for clubs seen in 6-8 matches per competition-season. Rue and Salvesen's 100-day memory (T2-04) was fitted only on second-half-of-season data, so it is not evidence for early-season weights. (4) An early-larger Elo K has only weak support (T2-09, +0.5% relative accuracy, one season, accuracy metric), and constant K=20 is the validated baseline (T2-08). (5) The prior's composition has one deployed precedent: 2/3 previous rating + 1/3 market value, with a small RPS gain (0.0011) from the market-value part, second-hand (T2-10).

missedEvidence: UEFA-specific, forecast-scored, pre-season-prior-only evidence: Csurilla and Csato, 'Match forecasts in UEFA club competitions: Elo ratings versus Transfermarkt valuations', arXiv:2609.21674, submitted 2026-09-18 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21674). Champions League and Europa League 2020/21-2024/25, 1,503 matches, expanding-window out-of-sample evaluation on 600 matches (238 in 2023/24, 362 in 2024/25), which includes the 2024/25 league phase (272 league-phase matches in the sample). Ratings are fixed at 1 September (club Elo, or lagged Transfermarkt value) with no in-season updating. Ordered probit, 100xRPS: historical frequencies 23.068, Elo 19.729, Transfermarkt 19.533, joint 19.539, equal-weight pool 19.431, estimated pool 19.480 (estimated Transfermarkt weight 0.35-0.40). Equal-weight pool beats Elo-only at p=0.045 but not Transfermarkt-only (p=0.499). Slope-stability tests for the 2024/25 league phase all have p between 0.238 and 0.866 (Table 8). This is a pre-season-prior-only score on UEFA matches. It says nothing about the blend with in-season results, so it supports 'a prior has value in UEFA' but not 'a current-season-only model fails'. It also gives an empirical Elo-vs-market-value combination result that bears on the second-hand 538 2/3 + 1/3 precedent in T2-10. It is a September 2026 preprint, not peer reviewed.

Heuer and Rubner 2014 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4157759/) has the numbers the researcher could not recover. (a) Text: 'After NY=12 matches the information contents of the previous season is basically equal to that of the first [12] matches of the present season.' (b) Table 2, regression weights on previous season vs first N_Y matches: N_Y 0/4/8/12/17 gives previous-season weight 3.71/3.20/2.60/2.23/1.86 and current-season weight 0/0.82/1.70/2.30/2.77. (c) Table 4, forecast K-value (a log-probability loss) for Bundesliga 2002/03-2006/07, first 10 match days vs all 34: home advantage only 1.073 / 1.057; + present-season matches 1.054 / 1.013; + previous season 1.027 / 1.004; + market value 1.019 / 1.000; Oddset 1.025 / 1.012. So adding the previous season cuts the loss by 0.027 in the first 10 match days vs 0.009 over the full season, and the full model matches the bookmaker odds (0.006 +/- 0.009 better, not significant) in that window. This is a measured early-season forecast-loss value of a carried-over prior in the researcher's own cited source. Caveats: chances-for-goals observable, Bundesliga only, K-value scale, not RPS.

Csato 2024, 'Club coefficients in the UEFA Champions League: Time for shift to an Elo-based formula' (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/24748668.2023.2274221, online 2023-11-07). 19 Champions League seasons 2003/04-2021/22, 1,824 group matches (1,402 decisive), Football Club Elo fixed at 30 June vs the UEFA club coefficient, logistic and multinomial regressions. Elo beats the club coefficient on explanatory power and AUC, and the coefficient adds nothing after Elo for matches. Explanatory fit rather than a held-out RPS, and I saw only a search excerpt, not the full text. It is a pre-season-rating-only result for UEFA group matches.

Foulley 2015, 'A simple Bayesian procedure for forecasting the outcomes of the UEFA Champions League matches', arXiv:1501.05831 (abstract read only). Cumulative probit where team strength is regressed on an external rating (UEFA club ranking or Football Club World Ranking), with priors updated each season from the previous season's posterior; 2013-14 application; FCWR-based adjustment beats UEFACR. A UEFA-specific Bayesian prior-carryover design, which the researcher's 'none found' missed. I have not read the full text, so I cannot report its scores.

A KU Leuven workshop paper, 'B-CLAD: A Bayesian Competition-Linked Attack-Defence Model' (https://dtai.cs.kuleuven.be/events/MLSA26/papers/MLSA26_paper_380.pdf; excerpt only): 15 domestic leagues plus the three UEFA competitions, 2020/21-2024/25, trained on four seasons and tested on 2024/25 (2,549 matches). On promoted-team matches RPS is 0.189 vs 0.199 for Dixon-Coles; on UEFA matches 0.200 vs 0.199 (log loss 0.961 vs 0.980). Overall it is not better than Dixon-Coles. Workshop paper, excerpt only, so low weight, but it shows cross-competition hierarchical priors being scored on UEFA matches.

Minor: 538 pre-season weights (2/3 end-of-season SPI, 1/3 market value) are corroborated by an MSc thesis and two blogs found in search results, but all trace to the same FiveThirtyEight methodology page (https://fivethirtyeight.com/methodology/how-our-club-soccer-predictions-work/, quoted by one blog), which I did not read directly.

claims.quantity: Out-of-sample 100xRPS (ordered probit, lower is better) on 600 UCL+UEL matches from 2023/24 and 2024/25 (includes the 2024/25 league phase), pre-season (1 September) ClubElo difference: 19.729, against 23.068 for an expanding-window outcome-frequency benchmark. Log loss 0.932 vs 1.029; Brier (mean over 3 outcomes) 0.183 vs 0.207. Transfermarkt-only 19.533; equal-weight Elo+Transfermarkt pool 19.431.
claims.context: Csurilla and Csato, arXiv 2609.21674 (page dated 2026-09-18; a preprint, no peer review shown). Ratings are fixed at 1 September and NOT updated within the season; expanding-window ordered probit with home-venue and competition/phase controls; the benchmark has no match-context controls. UCL and UEL only (no Conference League). Panel 2020/21-2024/25: 1,503 matches, 1,394 in the common sample, 272 league-phase matches. Pool vs Elo: -0.297 RPSx100 (p=0.045); pool vs Transfermarkt: -0.102 (p=0.499). The same paper's Table 8 finds no break in the Elo slope in the 2024/25 league phase (smallest p above 0.2), but the authors call this absence of evidence from a single season. Betting odds were deliberately not used, so this is not a market comparison.
claims.quote: According to Table 5, all of our strength models clearly outperform the unconditional historical benchmark. ... | Historical | 600 | 23.068 | 0.207 | 1.029 | 0.510 | ... | Elo | 600 | 19.729 | 0.183 | 0.932 | 0.558 |
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Re-read arxiv.org/html/2609.21674 in full. Table 5c (ordered probit, N=600) matches every figure: Historical 23.068 / 0.207 / 1.029; Elo 19.729 / 0.183 / 0.932; Transfermarkt 19.533; equal-weight pool 19.431. The quoted sentence and table rows are verbatim. Setup also matches: 238 + 362 = 600 evaluation matches (2023/24 and 2024/25), 1 September Elo, forecasts not updated within a season, and a historical benchmark with Laplace-smoothed outcome frequencies and no match-context controls. Brier is 1/(3N), so the 'mean over 3 outcomes' note is right. RPS is 1/(2N) times 100. Table 6 gives pool vs Elo -0.297 (p=0.045) and pool vs TM -0.102 (p=0.499). Table 8 is a single-season in-sample slope test on N=1394 with 272 league-phase matches; smallest p is 0.238, and the paper itself says 'absence of evidence'. Caveat that holds: the 19.7 vs 23.1 gap partly reflects controls the benchmark lacks, as the paper says.

claims.quantity: Share of UCL matches called correctly by 'higher rating wins', 2003/04-2021/22, ratings fixed before each season: group matches 73.32% (ClubElo at 30 June) vs 70.68% (UEFA club coefficient); two-legged knockout ties 65.00% vs 61.92%. Logistic AUC for decisive group matches (n=1,402 of 1,824) 0.814 (Elo) vs 0.784 (coefficient).
claims.context: Csato, Int. J. Performance Analysis in Sport 2023 (arXiv 2304.09078 read; T&F page also seen). UCL only, old 32-team group format, 19 seasons, 260 two-legged ties after removing six single-leg 2019/20 matches. The logistic samples exclude draws; the paper says the coefficient adds no significant information beyond Elo for group matches and knockout qualification, and (multinomial model including draws) is also insignificant once Elo is in. For group ranking the coefficient adds a small significant term in one specification and not in the alternative one. The sample base of Table 3's raw accuracy is not stated in the extract I read. The paper describes the coefficient as five seasons of points or the association coefficient, whichever is higher; I did not read UEFA's own regulations.
claims.quote: Crucially, the difference between Elo ratings robustly outperforms the difference between club coefficients. ... | Group matches | 70.68% | 73.32% | ... | Knockout qualification | 61.92% | 65.00% |
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Read the arXiv 2304.09078 v6 full text. Table 3 (70.68/73.32 group, 61.92/65.00 knockout), the AUCs of 0.784 and 0.814 (Table 4), n=1,402 of 1,824, and 260 ties after removing six 2019/20 single-leg matches all match, as do ClubElo fixed at 30 June and the coefficient definition. Elo-only vs coefficient: coefficient insignificant in Table 4 (0.003, SE 0.002), Table 5 (-0.007, SE 0.004) and Table 8; significant in Table 6 but not Table 7, as the researcher says. Quotes are verbatim. The researcher said the sample base of Table 3 is 'not stated'. It is resolvable: only 1,402 decisive group matches and 260 ties reproduce the percentages (1028/1402=73.32%, 991/1402=70.68%, 169/260, 161/260; no integer count over 1,824 gives 73.32%). So these are accuracies on decisive matches with draws excluded, not three-way accuracy on all UCL group matches. The T&F publication is dated 2024 (24(2)), DOI 2023.

claims.quantity: League-phase outcome shares home/draw/away, 144 matches per competition-season: UCL 2024/25 53.47/12.50/34.03%; UCL 2025/26 49.31/17.36/33.33%; UEL 2024/25 48.61/24.31/27.08%; UEL 2025/26 52.78/17.36/29.86%. Baselines in the same paper: UCL 2020/21-2023/24 (old format) 46.35/20.05/33.59%; top-4 domestic leagues 2023/24 43.91/26.42/29.67%.
claims.context: Winkelmann, Michels and Deutscher, arXiv 2508.20075 (fetched page; arXiv id suggests a first posting in Aug 2025, search metadata showed 2026-08-10, and it contains 2025/26 data, so a later version). Preprint. Draw counts stated in the text: 18 observed in 2024/25 and 25 in 2025/26 for the UCL. Authors' explanation for few UCL draws (weaker incentive to play for a draw) is a hypothesis, not tested there. Dixon-Coles fit on 2024/25 (n=144 each): home coefficient 0.296 (SE 0.094) UCL, 0.317 (SE 0.100) UEL on log goals; rho 0.102 (SE 0.096) UCL, 0.005 UEL, not significant. Conference League not covered. Only two league-phase seasons, so season-to-season swings of 5 points in draw share (UCL 12.5 to 17.4) are within what this sample cannot rule out as noise.

Table 7 matches: home 0.296 (0.094) and 0.317 (0.100), rho 0.102 (0.096) and 0.005 (SE 0.111). The 'markedly lower share of draws' quote is verbatim. Unflagged by the researcher: the old-format baseline includes the COVID behind-closed-doors 2020/21 season, which the paper itself caveats.

claims.quantity: Out-of-sample scores on the 2025/26 league phase (144 matches per competition) for a Dixon-Coles Poisson model with ClubElo difference fitted on 2024/25 only: UCL Brier 0.5262, RPS 0.3865, log score 0.8966; UEL Brier 0.5531, RPS 0.4088, log score 0.9412. UCL independent-Poisson: 0.5268 / 0.3868 / 0.8988.
claims.context: Winkelmann et al. arXiv 2508.20075, Table D1 (preprint). Training season 2024/25, test season 2025/26. The Brier and RPS values are on a different scale from T3-1: they are consistent with un-normalised sums (UCL Brier/3 = 0.175, RPS/2 = 0.193) but the passage I read does not state the normalisation (UNVERIFIED). No climatological baseline and no bookmaker score is reported in the passage read, so no skill figure is published there. Elo date for the covariate: 1 Sept of each season per the paper's Table 2 note.
claims.quote: The comparison is conducted out of sample, using the 2024/25 season as training data and the 2025/26 season as test data. ... | Brier Score | 0.5268 | 0.5262 | 0.5300 | 0.5533 | 0.5531 | 0.5574 | ... | RPS | 0.3868 | 0.3865 | 0.3883 | 0.4089 | 0.4088 | 0.4085 | ... | Log Score | 0.8988 | 0.8966 | 0.9074 | 0.9415 | 0.9412 | 0.9505 |
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: Table D1 is in Appendix D, past the first 60k characters of the page; I fetched the full page. Values match for all three scores in both competitions. The 'out of sample, 2024/25 train, 2025/26 test' sentence and the table rows are verbatim. The paper does not state the Brier/RPS normalisation. My own arithmetic supports the researcher's inference that these are un-normalised sums: climatological log loss on the 2025/26 UCL shares is 1.019 and RPS(/2) is about 0.236, so an RPS of 0.3865 on the /2 scale would be worse than climatology while the log score 0.8966 is better. That is arithmetic, not a statement in the paper. The text also notes bivariate Poisson has marginally the best UEL RPS (0.4085), which does not affect the logged D&C row.

claims.quantity: In UEFA two-legged knockout models, the UEFA club coefficient was significant while group-stage performance was not significant, alone or together with the coefficient (Eugster et al. 2011, reported by Geenens and Cuddihy).
claims.context: THIRD-PARTY REPORT: Geenens and Cuddihy (JRSS A 2018) describe Eugster et al. (2011); I did not read Eugster et al., so its sample, seasons and effect sizes are UNVERIFIED. Geenens and Cuddihy's own data are UCL and UEL results 2009/10-2014/15 (n=1,353 two-legged ties incl. qualifying rounds), away-goals era. They describe the coefficient as five seasons of points plus 20% of the country coefficient (since 2009). Their summary also states: 'A slight second-leg home advantage is evidenced.' (no magnitude read). Relevance: the only UEFA statement found on how much current-season performance adds to a carried-over rating, and it is about knockout rounds with a coefficient prior, not a league phase with 6-8 matches.
claims.quote: It turned out that ‘group stage performance’ was not statistically significant either in a model by itself or in a model which also used ‘club coefficient’ (which was significant).
claims.label: third-party-report
claims.skepticNote: The quote is verbatim in the OUP text of Geenens and Cuddihy (curly quotes aside). Also confirmed: n=1353, 2009/10-2014/15, qualifying rounds apparently included, 'since 2009 ... plus 20% of the relevant country coefficient', and 'A slight second-leg home advantage is evidenced'. The researcher's 'Eugster sample UNVERIFIED' is resolvable from the same paper: Eugster et al. covered only the final knockout stage of the UCL, 1994/95-2009/10. The same paper also rejects the logistic-model fit of Eugster-type models on its own data and says their underdog keeps about a 20% chance at maximum strength gap. So this null on group-stage performance is a hearsay null from a model the reporting paper criticises, with unknown power. Label 'third-party-report' is correct.

claims.quantity: FiveThirtyEight SPI pre-season rating = 2/3 end-of-previous-season SPI + 1/3 SPI implied by market value; reported RPS reduction of 0.0011 from adding market values (total domestic-league RPS 0.1957). Cross-league strengths: Massey's method on actual-minus-expected scores of inter-league matches, then regressed toward market-value-based ratings.
claims.context: THIRD-PARTY REPORT: slides by Clement Lee (sports-modelling reading group, dated 2023-04-28) summarising FiveThirtyEight. The primary page (fivethirtyeight.com/methodology/how-our-club-soccer-predictions-work/) could not be read: that URL returned an unrelated ABC News landing page and web.archive.org returned CONTENT_NOT_CACHED. Two other pages (a 2019 blog and a student project page) repeat 67%/33% but are not primary. The RPS figure is for 538's domestic forecasts, not UEFA matches; no UEFA-match evaluation of SPI found. This is a published pre-season prior recipe (last-season rating plus market value), not a weight between prior and in-season results. Whether SPI is still published was not checked.
claims.quote: 2/3 × end-of-season’s SPI + 1/3 × SPI implied by market value ... by 0.0011 using market values to pre-season SPI ... 4. Regress league strengths toward market-value based ratings
claims.label: third-party-report
claims.skepticNote: Core content verified verbatim in the Lee slides (2023-04-28): '2/3 x end-of-season's SPI + 1/3 x SPI implied by market value', 'Current RPS = 0.1957 after reductions ... by 0.0011 using market values to pre-season SPI', and 'Regress league strengths toward market-value based ratings'. The 2/3-1/3 split is also corroborated by other third-party pages (dadmetrics 2019: 67%/33%; Erasmus thesis 2022: 67%/33%). Not supported: the slides never say 0.1957 is a 'total domestic-league RPS' or that it excludes UEFA matches; that qualifier is the researcher's inference. The slides also give no definition of the RPS scale (they say 0 to 1). Primary 538 page still unread, so the label 'third-party-report' is right, but the domestic-league framing should be dropped or marked inferred.

claims.quantity: Probit model of progression in two-legged UEFA ties conditional on the first-leg scoreline, controlling for team and country strength, fitted on 6,975 contests; the value of a given first-leg result changed substantially over time and first-leg-home clubs became more likely to convert a given result into progression.
claims.context: Flores, Forrest, de Pablo and Tena, European Journal of Operational Research 2015; I read the abstract only (ResearchGate page, via search extract). Coefficients, seasons covered and whether qualifying rounds are included were not read. Away-goals era (the abstract refers to away goals as a tie-breaker), so not current rules. Geenens and Cuddihy (2018, Remark 1) argue Flores et al.'s second-leg-home-advantage inference is not valid because strength variables were set to their mean while first-leg-home teams are weaker on average; that is a third-party criticism I read but did not verify.
claims.quote: Employing data from 6,975 contests, modelling reveals that what constitutes a good result has changed substantially over time. Generally, clubs which play at home in the first leg have become more likely to convert any given first-leg result to eventual success.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: The quoted abstract text is verbatim on the Liverpool repository and ResearchGate pages: 6,975 contests, 'what constitutes a good result has changed substantially over time', and home-first clubs 'more likely to convert any given first-leg result'. The label 'verified-read' is generous: only the abstract was read, as the researcher disclosed, and the abstract does not say the probit was fitted on all 6,975 contests. The Liverpool press release says the data run from the 1960s away-goals era to 2012/13, so the finding predates current rules. The Geenens-Cuddihy Remark 1 criticism is real (read in the OUP text). Treat as abstract-only.

claims.quantity: 268 penalty shootouts in UEFA club competitions 2000/01 to end-2025 (207 in qualifying, 50 in knockout stage, 11 finals): no detectable effect of ClubElo strength (n=266; Elo-difference coefficient per 100 points -0.004, SE 0.069, p=0.959), shooting order, home field or comeback status; teams with at least 100 Elo points more fail to win 50% of shootouts.
claims.context: Csato and Petrozcy, Journal of Sports Economics (page metadata date 2025-10-20; text covers data to end of 2025; I did not reconcile the two). Read via search extract of the article text. Sample is dominated by qualifiers and recent seasons (139 of 268 in the last six). The authors state all earlier studies found stronger teams win more shootouts (Arrondel 2019, Krumer 2020, Wunderlich et al. 2020, Pipke 2025). I also read the Wunderlich et al. 2020 abstract (IJPAS, 1,067 shootouts from 14 cup competitions, betting-odds strength): 'winning probability remains around 40% even for very weak teams against very strong teams', i.e. a small effect in domestic cups. No quantitative extra-time model for UEFA ties was found.
claims.quote: the outcomes of the 268 penalty shootouts played in UEFA club competitions between 2000 and 2025 seem to be entirely unpredictable.
claims.label: verified-read
claims.skepticNote: The quote and the regression numbers come from arXiv v2 (2025-10-20/27), not the published paper at the cited DOI (JSE 2026, 27(6) 713-734). I read the arXiv text, which is v2 (latest is v6), and the author PDF at real.mtak.hu with JSE formatting. v2 intro: 'As we show, the outcomes of the 268 penalty shootouts ... seem to be entirely unpredictable.' The published text has no 'entirely' or 'unpredictable'. It says 'none of the variables above has a significant effect on winning', and the abstract hedges: coin-toss 'cannot be rejected'. v2 Table 2 has n=266, beta1=-0.004, SE 0.069, p=0.959. Published Table 2 uses 253 (extended) and 232 (restricted) home-away matches with strength coefficients around 0.019 (0.071) and 0.005 (0.075). Still true in both versions: 268 total, 207/50/11 split, 139 of 268 in the last six seasons, 266 Elo-usable shootouts in the baseline text, and teams 100+ Elo ahead failing to win 50% (v2 Table A.2: 73 of 154, 47.4%). The conclusion (no detectable Elo effect) survives; the cited quote and Table 2 figures do not belong to the cited version.

topics.designImplication: UEFA-specific evidence supports four design points and leaves the prior weight open. 1) Cross-league scale: a pre-season ClubElo-type rating beats the UEFA coefficient on UCL matches (T3-2), and a frozen 1-September Elo gives 100xRPS 19.7 against a 23.1 outcome-frequency benchmark on 600 UCL+UEL matches including the 2024/25 league phase (T3-1). So a prior built from carried-over Elo-style strength has direct UEFA support, and the Elo slope showed no detectable change in the new format (T3-1 context, one season). 2) Blend weight: I found no external study that gives one. The only UEFA statements are that a frozen pre-season rating is already useful, and a third-party report that group-stage performance added nothing beyond the coefficient in knockout rounds (T3-5, details unverified). The weight therefore has to come from the non-UEFA topics; UEFA evidence can only act as a sanity bound. 3) Benchmarks and calibration anchors: my own arithmetic from the T3-3 shares gives an in-sample climatological log loss of about 1.019 and RPS (divided by 2) of about 0.236 for the 2025/26 UCL league phase, against a published out-of-sample Elo Dixon-Coles log score of 0.8966 (T3-4); the climatology uses the test season's own frequencies, so it is generous to the baseline. The bookmaker log loss of 0.93-0.94 (T3-10) is on 60-64 matches from a commercial source and should not be treated as a market benchmark. Draw share was 12.5% and then 17.4% in the UCL, 24.3% and then 17.4% in the UEL, against 20% in the old UCL format and 26% in domestic leagues; home wins were 49-53% (T3-3). Winkelmann et al. found a domestic-league-trained model predicted about 31 draws against 18 observed, so draw and home constants should not be copied from domestic leagues, and with n=144 per competition-season they should be treated as ranges. 4) Two-legged ties: the published structure is progression conditioned on the first-leg score plus strength (T3-7), with historical base rates that include the away-goals era (T3-9); shootouts in UEFA club competition are indistinguishable from a coin flip with n=266 (T3-8), while a domestic-cup study finds about 40% for the weaker side. Do not use pre-2021 tie rates as current-rules rates.
